---

## 1. The reframe I'd start from

So the sub-2% conversion rate probably isn't a paywall-design failure. It's an artifact of offering one price to a population whose willingness to pay likely spans two orders of magnitude.

The working thesis: **let each segment pay in the currency it actually has surplus of.** Some have money. Some have attention. Some have time and contribution. Some have reach. Some are embedded inside an organization that has a budget they've never been asked about. A single-currency monetization model leaves most of that on the table while irritating everyone.

Grandfather existing habit permanently. The free tier isn't charity — it's the distribution engine, the ratings shield, and the top of every funnel below.

---

## 3. The mix, and why each piece earns its place

### 3.1 Subscriptions — three tiers, not one

The single-tier structure is very likely the specific cause of the 2% ceiling. A three-tier ladder does two things at once: it captures Segment A/B surplus that a $8 price point was quietly discarding, and it opens a low-friction door for Segment C.

- **Plus (~$3.49/mo, or $27/yr)** — friction removal and personalization, not capability gating: ad-free, higher soft quotas, customization/status goods, offline, faster processing. Sold *annual-first*; the psychology of a low annual number ($27) outperforms a low monthly number, and annual buyers churn a fraction as much.
- **Pro (~$11.99/mo, or $99/yr)** — depth: advanced features, high or unbounded quotas, exports, integrations, history/archive, priority compute.
- **Teams/Business (~$20/seat/mo, min 3 seats, or platform + usage)** — shared workspaces, admin, permissions, audit, API, SLA-flavored support.

The Teams line is the one I'd bet is most underestimated. In consumer apps with millions of users there is nearly always a hidden B2B business — a few thousand small teams already coordinating around the product with duct tape. It converts at 10–30x consumer rates, churns less, and expands. It also produces revenue that doesn't touch a single free user's experience, which is exactly the kind of revenue you need right now.

A quiet efficiency: price the middle tier so that Pro is the obvious choice for anyone who does the maths, and set Teams so that three Pro seats cost more than a Teams plan. Ladders work when each rung makes the next one look cheap.

### 3.2 Usage-based — the piece that's probably missing entirely

Segments D and much of C will not sign a recurring commitment, and pushing them toward one is precisely what produced the uninstall spike. But they will pay for a specific outcome at the moment of need — willingness to pay peaks at the point of intent and decays within minutes.

- **Credit packs**: $2.99 / $7.99 / $17.99 with declining unit prices. Credits never expire (expiry generates complaints far out of proportion to the revenue it protects).
- **Day/Week Pass**: $1.99 / $4.99 — full Pro for a bounded window. This is the highest-converting product most consumer apps never ship.
- **Metered premium capability**: attach consumption pricing to the genuinely expensive-to-serve operations (AI inference, large exports, storage, priority processing). This does double duty — it monetizes *and* it aligns your cost curve with your revenue curve, which speaks directly to the loss problem rather than only the revenue problem.
- **Ladder mechanic**: when a user's trailing 90-day credit spend crosses the subscription break-even, surface a single, honest message: *"You've spent $34 on packs. Plus would have been $27."* Trust converts better than pressure, and it doesn't generate reviews.

### 3.3 Advertising — the same idea reconstructed

Ads damaged ratings before, and I wouldn't conclude ads are the problem. Interstitials, cold-start ads, and mediated ad-network inventory are the problem. What I'd rebuild:

- **Rewarded and opt-in only, at first.** Attention exchanged for credits, quota, or a temporary Pro unlock — user-initiated, so it registers as generosity rather than tax. This is also the natural monetization for Segment C, who would rather spend attention than money.
- **Native commerce / intent-matched placements** inside surfaces that already exist. If any part of the product involves discovery, comparison, or planning, there's affiliate and marketplace revenue with a positive user experience.
- **Sponsored content** in existing content slots, held to the same editorial quality bar as organic — indistinguishable in quality, clearly labelled in provenance.
- Later, if commerce intent is real: **first-party ad/retail-media platform** with direct advertiser relationships. Higher CPMs, controllable creative quality, no arbitrage junk.

Hard constraints I'd bake into the ad layer as code, not policy:

1. No ads for the first 14 days or first 10 sessions of a user's life.
2. No interstitials, ever, on cold start or app open.
3. No ads on failure, error, or empty states.
4. No ads for any paying user, on any tier, including expired-but-recently-paid.
5. Frequency caps enforced per-user-per-day, with a global creative quality floor and category blocklist.
6. Every unit carries "hide / why this ad."
7. Zero ads for Segment F.
8. Ad load ramps by *engagement tier*, never uniformly.

Most rating collapses come from #2, #3, and creative quality — not ad presence.

- **Employer / education / insurer benefit channels**, if the product touches productivity, health, learning, or finance. Someone else's budget, your product, no consumer price sensitivity.
- **Embedded licensing (B2B2C)**: the product, or one capability of it, as a feature inside a larger platform. Longer sales cycle, but it converts your engineering into a second business line.
- **Commerce and affiliate**, wherever there's natural purchase intent.
- **Aggregate insight products** — consented, privacy-safe, aggregated only, with a public policy. Handled carelessly this is an existential reputational risk; handled well it's high-margin. I'd sequence it last and only with an explicit, legible consent posture. Worth asking whether the revenue justifies the trust exposure at all.

Today: ~2% × ~$8 ≈ **$0.16 blended ARPU/month.**

|---|---|---|
| Plus | 4.0% | $0.14 |
| Pro | 1.8% | $0.22 |
| Teams (seats) | 0.15% | $0.03 |
| Usage/credits/passes | 7% of non-subs paying ~$4.50/qtr | $0.10 |
| Rewarded + native ads | ~55% of free base | $0.18 |
| Commerce/affiliate | — | $0.06 |
| Partnerships (contracted) | — | $0.09 |
| **Blended** | | **≈ $0.82** |

### 5.1 Architectural decisions that come before any test

- **Permanent global holdout, 5%.** Never monetized, never touched. It's the only way to measure the *cumulative* long-run cost of everything you ship, and it's what lets you answer "is monetization eroding the base?" with evidence in eighteen months instead of an argument.

- **Automated circuit breakers.** Every monetization surface behind a flag that any on-call engineer can pull in under an hour without a meeting. Speed of reversal is a bigger determinant of downside than accuracy of forecast.
- **Willingness-to-pay research in parallel**, not before: Van Westendorp for range, Gabor-Granger for elasticity, conjoint for bundle composition — run per segment. Cheap, fast, and it stops you burning live tests on price points research would have eliminated.

### 5.2 Sequencing — additive before subtractive, always

**Phase 0 (weeks 1–4): instrument, don't ship.** Segment clustering, cost-to-serve per segment, WTP study, shadow-price the existing base, stand up the holdout and the guardrail dashboard with alerting.

**Phase 1 (weeks 3–10): pure upside.** Partnerships (no user impact), Teams/Business tier for Segment A (new capability, new audience), annual plan for existing subscribers, regional pricing. Every one of these is additive — nothing is taken from anyone. Expect meaningful revenue with near-zero retention risk. Also buys political room for the harder phases.

**Phase 2 (weeks 8–18): the ladder.** Plus/Pro tier restructure, credit packs, Day/Week Pass, rewarded value exchange. Tests are on *placement and timing* of offers, not on removing capability. The core question here is contextual: which moment of intent converts without irritating? My prior is post-success moments convert 2–4x better than pre-task blocks and generate a fraction of the negative sentiment.

**Phase 3 (weeks 16–30): quota calibration.** Only now do you touch free-tier limits — and only on *new* users and *new* capabilities, never retroactively on existing habit. Geo-isolated, one variable at a time.

**Phase 4 (weeks 24+): ad layer.** Last, slowest, most instrumented. Geo-isolated cells, 1% → 5% → 20% → 50% ramps with a full 28-day observation window between steps. Ratings are a global, lagging, hard-to-reverse asset; treat ad expansion as irreversible even though the flag is technically reversible.

### 5.3 Test design specifics

- **Unit of randomization**: user-level for paywalls and tiers; **geo/market-level for advertising and ratings-sensitive changes**, since reviews and word-of-mouth leak across users and contaminate user-level cells.
- **Duration**: minimum two full natural usage cycles plus a 28-day post-exposure tail. Episodic segments (D) need 60–90 days — anything shorter systematically overstates their tolerance because you never observe the return visit that doesn't happen.
- **Measurement**: cohort-level retention curves, not session metrics. Revenue read on a *net* basis — incremental subscription revenue minus lost ad revenue minus modelled retention loss valued at LTV.
- **Statistics**: pre-registered primary metric and segment hypotheses; sequential testing with alpha spending so daily monitoring is legitimate; **deliberately asymmetric thresholds** — require p<0.05 to ship a revenue win, but act on p<0.10 for a retention harm. Stopping is cheap; being wrong about churn compounds.
- **Ratings lag is the central measurement problem.** Reviews arrive 1–3 weeks after the experience that caused them. Leading proxies: in-app sentiment micro-surveys, uninstall-flow free text, support ticket topic classification, review-text topic model on the 1% cell, and 72-hour post-exposure uninstall rate. Treat the store rating itself as a *confirmation* metric, never as your detector.

### 5.4 Guardrails and kill thresholds

| Metric | Read | Warn | **Kill** |
|---|---|---|---|
| D7 retention, by segment | daily, cohort |

Introducing a $3.49 tier without a migration and fencing plan risks a large fraction of them stepping down. The plan says "grandfather habit" but never models switching. There must be an explicit answer: are legacy subscribers price-locked, auto-mapped to Pro at legacy pricing, or offered an annual upgrade incentive? And the ARPU table should show legacy-base cannibalization as a negative line.

**2.4 Rewarded ads and credit sales are double-counted.** Rewarded ads pay out in credits; credits are also sold for cash. Every rewarded-ad grant suppresses a credit purchase. The model counts $0.18 of ad revenue and $0.10 of usage revenue with no cannibalization term. Real-world substitution in rewarded economies runs 20–50%. Either net it out or design a hard sink (rewarded credits usable only on a restricted subset of actions).

**2.5 The 2%→6% subscriber penetration jump is asserted, not bridged.** Tripling paid penetration in 12 months is at the aggressive end of what tier restructuring delivers. Show the bridge: exposure lift × offer-mix lift × price-point elasticity, per segment, with the WTP study as the input. Right now "unremarkable for a well-segmented consumer app, and therefore credible" is doing the work that arithmetic should do.

**2.6 Segment shares don't close.** Upper bounds sum to 118%, which makes "F = remainder" negative. Cosmetic, but it undermines confidence in the quantitative sections.

**2.7 Currency inconsistency.** €40/month in Section 1, dollars everywhere else. Trivial, but it reads as a stitched-together draft.

---

## 3. Feasibility errors on timing

**3.1 Partnerships are mis-sequenced as fast revenue.** Carrier, OEM, ISP, and bank bundles are described as "structurally the cleanest revenue you can add this quarter." They are not. Those deals routinely run 9–18 months: procurement, revenue-share negotiation, billing integration, security review, launch marketing. The plan puts them in Phase 1 (weeks 3–10) and books $0.09 ARPU inside 12 months. Realistically, first material carrier revenue lands in month 12–18. Employer/education channels are faster (3–6 months) but still not this quarter. Fix: split partnerships into *near-term* (affiliate/commerce, which can ship in weeks; embedded API pilots) and *long-cycle* (carrier/OEM), and remove the long-cycle revenue from the 12-month model.

**3.2 The timeline ignores the stated constraint.** The brief says investor patience is ending. Ads — the second-largest line at $0.18 — don't begin ramping until week 24 and reach 50% traffic sometime past week 40. Nothing in the plan tells the board what revenue lands in **Q1**. This needs a quarterly ramp with a runway overlay, and an explicit statement of which levers are cash-positive inside 90 days. Candidates the document omits entirely (see §4).

**3.3 Phase 2's own duration rule is violated.** Section 5.3 requires 60–90 day tests for episodic Segment D. Phase 2 runs weeks 8–18 (10 weeks) and includes credit packs and passes, which are *the* Segment D products. The schedule cannot deliver the required read.

---

## 4. Material omissions

Ranked by value-to-effort, these are the gaps I'd flag hardest — several are faster and safer than anything in Phase 1:

- **Involuntary churn and dunning recovery.** Payment failures typically cause 20–40% of subscription churn. Smart retries, card-updater, grace periods, and localized payment methods recover a meaningful slice at **zero retention or ratings risk**. This should be Phase 1, week 1.
- **Cancellation flow / save offers** — pause, downgrade-to-Plus, discount, plan-switch. Directly counters the "aggressive paywall" problem by giving unhappy payers an exit that isn't uninstall.
- **Family and multi-user consumer plans.** Proven ARPU-accretive and retention-*positive*; absent from a plan that otherwise covers every packaging axis.
- **Rating recovery mechanics.** The ratings were already damaged. There's no plan to repair them: review-prompt timing gated on success moments and high-NPS cohorts, developer responses to negative reviews, store-listing refresh. Ratings are an asset you can actively rebuild, not just protect.
- **ATT / IDFA / signal loss.** iOS ad ARPU is 40–70% below Android in most categories. The $0.18 ad line needs a platform split and an ATT opt-in assumption. Similarly, EU DMA/GDPR consent posture affects both ads and the insight product.
- **Cost-to-serve and gross margin.** The brief's problem is *losses*, not just revenue. Metered pricing on AI inference is mentioned as cost-aligning, but there's no COGS-per-segment analysis, no free-tier cost ceiling, and no answer to "what does a Segment E lurker cost us per month, and does $0.33 of ad ARPU cover it?" For some apps, *reducing cost-to-serve on unmonetizable segments* beats monetizing them.
- **The "reach" and "contribution" currencies are dangling.** Section 1 promises segments can pay in reach and contribution; the offer map contains no referral-credit, creator-revenue-share, or UGC-for-credits mechanic. Either operationalize it or drop the claim.
- **Segment D vs. F is operationally ambiguous.** Both are defined by long gaps. D is your usage-revenue engine; F is excluded from all monetization. Misclassification either kills revenue or buys one-star reviews. Needs a concrete classifier — inter-arrival-time *distribution stability* (healthy episodic) versus *monotonic decline in trailing frequency* (dormant), with a stated confidence threshold and a default-to-F tie-break.
- **Minors/students.** Segment C explicitly includes students. If any users are under 16/13, COPPA/GDPR-K constrain both ad targeting and subscription flows. Unaddressed.
- **Credits never expiring** creates an unbounded deferred-revenue liability and an accounting/breakage treatment question. Defensible UX call, but flag it to finance.

---

## 5. Experiment design critique

Much of §5 is genuinely good — the permanent holdout, pre-registered segment dimensions, asymmetric significance thresholds (p<0.05 to ship, p<0.10 to kill), and treating store rating as confirmation rather than detector are all correct and non-obvious. Specific weaknesses:

- **Geo-level randomization has a power problem the document doesn't acknowledge.** With market-level cells you have N in the low tens, not millions. Naive t-tests on geo cells will be badly underpowered against exactly the small retention harms you're trying to catch. This requires matched-market pairing, synthetic control / difference-in-differences, or a switchback design — plus an explicit statement of the minimum detectable effect. Right now "geo-isolated" is asserted as a solution when it's a new inference problem.
- **The holdout is contaminated and over-claimed.** Word-of-mouth, ratings, and shared-content effects leak into a 5% user-level holdout, so it measures the *individual-exposure* effect, not the cumulative brand effect. It also cannot serve as the control for geo-level ad tests. Say what it can and cannot answer.
- **No LTV model, despite the measurement rule depending on one.** "Revenue read on a net basis — minus modelled retention loss valued at LTV" requires a stated, per-segment LTV with a discount rate and a documented churn curve. Without it, the net-revenue rule is unfalsifiable and will be argued rather than computed.

The strategy has four moves, deliberately ordered so that the earliest revenue carries the least retention risk:

1. **Fix the leaks before adding pressure** (Q1). Involuntary churn recovery, cancellation save offers, annual-plan migration, web checkout where legally available, affiliate commerce. All of this is additive, none of it is visible to a free user as a new tax, and it is the only part of the plan that lands inside 90 days.
2. **Replace one price with a ladder and a meter** (Q2–Q3). Three subscription tiers plus family, and — the piece I believe is genuinely missing — usage-based pricing for the large episodic segment that will never sign a recurring commitment.
3. **Build a second business quietly** (Q2–Q4, extending beyond). Teams/Business for the commercial users already inside the consumer base; near-term embedded/API partnerships. Revenue that touches no free user's experience at all.
4. **Rebuild the ratings asset, then and only then re-approach advertising** (Q3–Q4). Rewarded and native only, behind hard-coded constraints, gated on a ratings-recovery precondition.

**What I am least confident about, and would want the group to pressure-test:** the 2% → 5.3% penetration bridge (§6), the advertising ARPU assumption given iOS signal loss (§5.4), and whether we have the organizational bandwidth to run this many parallel workstreams without the quality of any one of them slipping.

## 1. Before we prescribe: the diagnosis we owe ourselves

I had originally written that the single-tier price structure was the cause of the 2% ceiling. On reflection that was a hypothesis wearing the clothes of a finding, and I'd rather withdraw it than defend it. There are at least four explanations for a 2% conversion rate, and they imply completely different plans:

| Hypothesis | Test | If true, the plan changes to… |
|---|---|---|
| **Exposure** — most users never see a paid offer | Decompose: MAU → paywall impression → trial start → paid → retained M3 | Offer placement and contextual triggering, not pricing. Cheapest fix in the document. |
| **Activation** — users never reach the moment that makes payment rational | Correlate paid conversion with reaching each core value milestone; measure milestone attainment rate | Onboarding and time-to-value work precedes all packaging work |
| **Price/packaging** — the offer is mispriced or mis-fenced for most of the base | WTP study per segment; price-point elasticity | The ladder in §4 |
| **Mechanics** — trial→paid leakage, payment failures, no save path | Billing funnel audit, dunning report, cancellation flow audit | §3, and it's nearly free |

**This decomposition takes roughly two days of analyst time and I would not want us to commit to anything else until it's done.** `[D]` If exposure turns out to be, say, 20% of MAU, then we are converting ~10% of exposed users — which is a healthy offer with a distribution problem, and half of the packaging work below becomes lower priority. I'd rather discover that in week one than in month six.

I've written the rest of the document as though price/packaging and exposure both matter, because that is my prior `[A]`. But the sequencing in §7 is built so that the diagnosis can redirect us without wasting work.

---

## 2. The framing I'd propose we adopt

Both prior tests share a structure worth noticing: they taxed *everyone equally* for value that is *distributed very unequally*. A paywall that lands on a user receiving $40/month of value is a bargain; the same paywall on a user receiving $0.50 of value reads as an insult, and insulted users do not leave quietly — they leave a review.

The working thesis I'd like us to align on: **let each segment pay in the currency it has a surplus of.** Some users have money. Some have attention. Some have time and willingness to contribute. Some have reach. Some sit inside an organization with a budget nobody has ever asked them about. A single-currency model leaves most of that uncollected while irritating everyone.

Two constraints I would treat as non-negotiable, because the uninstall spike already proved the first and the ratings damage proved the second:

1. **Never charge for what a user already has.** We monetize depth, new headroom, and cost-to-serve. Existing habit is grandfathered permanently. The free tier is not charity — it is the distribution engine, the ratings shield, and the top of every funnel beneath it.
2. **Never monetize a user who is already leaving.** More on this in §3.3.
